what_its_for: Vilazodone is used to treat depression (major depressive disorder) in adults. It helps improve your mood, sleep, appetite, and energy levels, and reduces feelings of sadness, anxiety, and hopelessness.
how_to_take: Take vilazodone by mouth ONCE a day WITH FOOD. Taking it with food is very important — it helps your body absorb the medicine properly. If you take it on an empty stomach, it may not work as well. Try to take it at the same time every day to help you remember. You can take it in the morning or evening, whichever works best for you. Swallow the tablet whole.
dosing: Your doctor will usually start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over a few weeks. The typical starting dose is 10 mg once daily for 7 days, then increased to 20 mg once daily for 7 days, and then to the usual dose of 40 mg once daily. Never change your dose or stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal-like symptoms such as dizziness, nausea, headache, or irritability.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but ONLY if it is still the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at once or double up to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store vilazodone at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about medicine take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking vilazodone, as it can increase dizziness, drowsiness, and other side effects. Do not take vilazodone with MAO inhibitors (such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, linezolid, or methylene blue) — this combination can cause a dangerous and potentially life-threatening reaction called serotonin syndrome. Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAO inhibitor and starting vilazodone. Be cautious with other medications that affect serotonin, such as triptans, tramadol, lithium, or St. John's Wort, as they may increase your risk of serotonin syndrome. Use caution when driving or operating machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it may cause dizziness or drowsiness. Avoid taking NSAIDs (like ibuprofen or aspirin) or blood thinners unless your doctor approves, as vilazodone may increase your risk of bleeding.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: thoughts of suicide or self-harm, new or worsening depression or anxiety, unusual mood changes or agitation, signs of serotonin syndrome (agitation, fast heartbeat, high fever, muscle twitching, sweating, shivering, or diarrhea), severe allergic reaction (rash, swelling of face or throat, difficulty breathing), unusual bleeding or bruising, seizures, low sodium symptoms (headache, confusion, weakness, unsteady feeling), or painful or prolonged erections (priapism). Also call your doctor if side effects like nausea, diarrhea, or dizziness are bothering you or not going away.
when_it_works: Most people do not feel the full benefits right away. You may start to notice some improvement in sleep, appetite, or energy within the first 1 to 2 weeks. However, it may take 4 to 8 weeks of regular use to feel the full antidepressant effect. Do not stop taking the medicine if you do not feel better right away — be patient and keep taking it as prescribed. Let your doctor know if you do not notice any improvement after several weeks.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before taking vilazodone if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Taking antidepressants during the last trimester of pregnancy may cause temporary withdrawal symptoms or breathing problems in the newborn. Breastfeeding: Vilazodone may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits before breastfeeding. Children and Teenagers: Vilazodone is not approved for use in children or teenagers under 18 years old. Young adults (18 to 24 years old) should be monitored closely for increased thoughts of suicide, especially at the start of treatment or after dose changes. Older Adults (65+): Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects such as dizziness and low sodium levels (hyponatremia). They should be monitored closely. Kidney or Liver Problems: Generally, no dose adjustment is needed for mild to moderate kidney or liver issues, but your doctor may monitor you more closely. Tell your doctor about all your health conditions before starting this medicine.
